title: CHAPTER TWO. On the grace of redemption; incarnation and the person of Christ
english: CHAPTER TWO. On the grace of redemption: where of the incarnation and person of Christ.

Thus far concerning the grace of paternal mercy: there follows the grace of fraternal redemption, which is the second principle of our salvation, by which the Son of God, as philanthropic mediator, reconciled the fallen human race to His Father, justice being kept safe, according to the order and promise of the new grace.

For the grace of mercy explained in the preceding chapter is so arranged that the parts of divine justice, by which He hates and punishes sin, nevertheless remain whole, and nothing is derogated from it by Gods mercy. That this might be satisfied, it was necessary that the Son of God Himself put on human nature, so that a human might satisfy for humans and God might thus put a certain infinite force into this satisfaction. For infinite justice injured by us could be satisfied only by an obedience and passion in some way infinite. This grace is immense, as David testifies in Psalm 49:8-9.
II. Here are to be considered the incarnation, office, state, and satisfaction of the person of Christ.

title: III. Incarnation defined; personal subsistence communicated to the assumed nature
english: III. Incarnation is that by which the eternal Son of God, human nature having been assumed into the unity of person, at a definite time was made human from a woman, that He might act as mediator between God and humans. Its foundations are shown in Psalm 45:8; Isaiah 7:14; 1 Peter 1:20; John 1:14; Matthew 1:21 and 16:16; Galatians 4:4; 1 John 4:2; 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 2:14. Of this grace the Apostle asserts in 1 Timothy 3:16 that it is the great mystery of godliness.

This incarnation, as we learn from the Scriptures, took place thus: the Holy Spirit coming upon the blessed virgin Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowing her, she conceived and bore the Son of God — that is, an individual and singular human nature, which without male seed, by the omnipotent power common to the Son with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the virgin had conceived, and which the Son assumed into the unity of person, or, what amounts to the same, personally united to Himself and communicated to that human nature the ultimate substantial term and degree by which an intelligent nature is completed in the category of being

For since a person is a rational nature as incommunicable substance, we call personality that very thing by which a person is constituted in the ultimate and complete personal being, and by which it is made incommunicable. Such personality the nature conceived from the virgin could have had of itself; but lest there be two persons rather than one, the Son of God therefore communicated His own to it and terminated the assumed nature by His first and intimate personal perfection, completed it substantially, and constituted it in the ultimate hypostatic and incommunicable being.

title: IV–VI. Truth of the two natures in the incarnate person; divine and human
english: IV. In the incarnate person of Christ are contemplated the truth of the two natures, divine and human, and their personal union.

V. The divine nature in Christ is that by which He Himself, the eternal Son of God, personally united human nature to Himself. The divine nature, as the Leiden theologians rightly teach (Synopsis, disputation XXV, thesis 9), is not here properly understood as incarnate insofar as it is common to the three persons, but insofar as it is the Sons, distinct by a singular mode of subsistence — not as if the Deity of the Father and of the Holy Spirit were other and other, but because the Word of the essence is distinctly considered in the Son as communicated to Him from the Father by eternal generation (1 Timothy 3:16; Colossians 2:9; Proverbs 8:22-23; John 1:1,14; 8:58; Philippians 2:6). Orthodox theologians demonstrate this most solidly against Photinians, Arians, Servetists, and Socinians.

VI. The human nature in Christ is that which, absolute in all its essential parts and properties, was assumed by Him from the flesh of the virgin Mary into the unity of person. From this nature the Son of God is called made flesh (John 1:14) by synecdoche, as a whole human consisting of a true body and a rational soul — and indeed not excluding the humble and miserable condition and origin of humans (Philippians 2:7; John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Hebrews 2:14; 4:15). Hence His genealogy is also led to Adam (Luke 3:38), against Marcion and the Manichees who invent Christs body as only apparent and simulated, and against the Valentinians who deny that Christ assumed His flesh from the substance of the virgin mother. Because He is a true human, He will have what constitutes a humans essence and without which to be human would involve a contradiction: namely an animated body and a rational soul endowed with intellect and will.

title: VII–X. Conception, assumption, and nativity of the human nature
english: VII. Further, of the human nature are considered conception, assumption, and nativity.

VIII. Conception is that by which, by a singular operation of the Holy Spirit, it began to exist in the womb of the virgin Mary from her own seed. This is taught in Genesis 3:15; Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:18,20; Luke 1:30-31 — and indeed supernaturally and by the immediate power of the Holy Spirit, in respect of which He is singularly called not begotten but made (Romans 1:3; Galatians 4:4), and holy (Luke 1:34-35; Hebrews 7:26), and is compared with the first Adam not as to the matter of the body but as to the mode of conception (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:45,47).

IX. The assumption of human nature by the Word is that by which the Son of God, at the very first moment of conception, bestowed His own personality on that human substance in Marys womb that was properly without subsistence or personality. For Leo the Great rightly says (epistle XI): Our nature was not so assumed that it was first created and afterward assumed, but that it was created by the very assumption — lest anyone suppose the humanity existed before it was united to the Word. Compare Hebrews 2:16; Colossians 2:9; Philippians 2:7.

X. Nativity is that by which the Son of God was brought forth into the light as a true human from the virgin Mary at the mature and lawful time of birth. From the prediction of Moses (Genesis 49:10) and of Isaiah 7:14; Micah 5:2; Luke 2:6-7,22-23 teaches Christs birth, as also Paul in Galatians 4:4.

title: XI–XIII. Personal union; ineffable mode neither essential nor accidental
english: XI. Personal union is that by which the Son of God joined the assumed nature to Himself into the unity of His person. XII. In it are contemplated mode and effect.

XIII. Although the mode is ineffable, it is denied to be a conjunction or union that is either essential — by which things having a mutual and natural respect to one another are united, as act and potency, matter and form, genus and specific difference — or accidental, by which either accidents are joined to subjects or substances themselves are accidentally joined among themselves: but personal, by which in the personality of the Word as a common bond distinct natures, not inclining by any natural tendency to union, are gathered into one — a union whose like is not found in the whole nature of things — against Eutyches confusing the natures and Nestorius tearing them apart and wrongly dissolving the unity of Christs person.
Since therefore there is one personality of both natures, there is also one person and one personal union (1 Corinthians 8:6; John 20:31; 1 John 4:15; John 9:37).

title: XIV. Effect of the union: communion of natures and communication of idioms; Cap.2 close toward Cap.3
english: XIV. The effect of the personal union is the communion both of the natures and of the properties, which is called the communication of idioms. On account of it they are predicated of one another — not absolutely and abstractly, but through concrete words that involve the supposit and connote the personality in which the natures agree. For the reason why one nature is predicated of the other is none other than the hypostatic union in the same supposit.

Therefore it is unlawful to say absolutely that God suffered, or that a human created heaven; but through concretes one is rightly declared of the other, and the property and operation of the one of the other — as God is human, the human is God, God suffered and died, the human is eternal and made heaven and earth. Damascene calls this an exchange of names, and Melanchthon defines the predication in which a property belonging to one nature is attributed to the person in the concrete. For just as the unity of person and the personal union, so also the distinction of the two natures in Christ is necessarily retained. And because the idioms of both natures are attributed indifferently to the person signified by concrete words, therefore on account of the difference of natures it is sometimes usual to add according to which nature the predicate belongs to the subject.
